method: USDA consumer weight classes are minimum net weights per dozen in the shell, so the tool converts through the per-egg equivalent of the class: the dozen minimum in ounces (Peewee 15, Small 18, Medium 21, Large 24, Extra large 27, Jumbo 30) multiplied by 28.349523125 and divided by 12. Large is therefore 56.699 g, Extra large 63.786 g, Medium 49.611 g, Small 42.524 g, Peewee 35.437 g and Jumbo 70.874 g. In count mode the recipe's weight is its egg count times the per-egg equivalent of the recipe's class. In weight mode the entered grams of egg are that weight directly, so a recipe written as 150 g of egg can be turned into a number of eggs. The number of eggs you need is that weight divided by the per-egg equivalent of the size you have; the page also reports the total weight to weigh, the whole eggs rounded down with the weight they fall short, and the whole eggs rounded up with the weight they overshoot, plus the total in ounces. A whole number carries a 1e-9 tolerance so an exact match is not printed as 2.9999 eggs. Counts are limited to 0.25-60 eggs with up to two decimals, weights to 5-3400 g with up to two decimals, and both sizes must be one of the six USDA classes. Every weight includes the shell and assumes the class minimum per egg, while the legal class describes the carton rather than one egg, and real eggs vary, so weighing cracked eggs is more accurate than counting. The tool does not convert volume, separate yolks and whites, grade eggs, or assess quality, freshness or safety. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: USDA AMS shell egg weight classes are minimum net weights per dozen: Jumbo 30 oz, Extra large 27 oz, Large 24 oz, Medium 21 oz, Small 18 oz and Peewee 15 oz.

USDA Agricultural Marketing Service, Egg-Grading Manual (Agriculture Handbook 75), Table 5 prints the weight classes per dozen and per 30-dozen case, with the individual-egg minimum expressed at the rate per dozen.
One avoirdupois ounce is 28.349523125 grams, so a class minimum per dozen divides by 12 to give the per-egg equivalent used here.
Recipes conventionally assume Large eggs; the same per-dozen weights give the equivalent count in any other USDA class.
